draft.title: Matrix recurrence relations
card: A matrix recurrence relation builds each state matrix from the one before it. S(n+1) = T × S(n), where S(0) is the starting state matrix.
To find S(1), work out T × S(0). To find S(2), work out T × S(1). The matrix T always comes first in the product.
A column matrix B can be added at each step: S(n+1) = T × S(n) + B. Work out the product first, then add B.
draft.remember: Each state matrix comes from the one just before it: multiply by T, then add any column.

a.q: A recurrence relation is S(n+1) = T × S(n). Which calculation gives S(2)?
a.why: Each state matrix comes from the one before it, so S(2) comes from S(1), with T written first. T × S(0) would give S(1) instead.
a.clue: S(2) is built from the state matrix just before it.

b.q: A fish pond has S(n+1) = T × S(n) + B, with T = [0.8 0.3; 0.2 0.7], B = [10; 0] and S(0) = [200; 100]. What is S(1)?
b.why: T × S(0) = [0.8×200 + 0.3×100; 0.2×200 + 0.7×100] = [190; 110]. Adding B gives [200; 110]. The option [190; 110] leaves out B, and [200; 120] adds it to the wrong row.
b.clue: Multiply by T first, then add B to the first row only.

problems.detail: The why says [200; 120] 'adds it to the wrong row'. Adding 10 to the second row instead would give [190; 120]. The option [200; 120] actually adds 10 to both rows.

The clue 'add B to the first row only' suggests B is added to one row. In fact the whole column B = [10; 0] is added; the second row just gains 0. This could mislead students about how matrix addition works.

check.summary: The card and both intended answers are correct. The why for (b) misdescribes the [200; 120] distractor, which adds 10 to both rows, not the wrong row. The clue for (b) wrongly suggests B is added to the first row only, when the whole column is added.

final.title: Matrix recurrence relations
card: A matrix recurrence relation builds each state matrix from the one before it. \(S_{n+1} = TS_{n}\), where \(S_{0}\) is the starting state matrix.
To find \(S_{1}\), work out \(TS_{0}\). To find \(S_{2}\), work out \(TS_{1}\). The matrix \(T\) always comes first in the product.
A column matrix \(B\) can be added at each step: \(S_{n+1} = TS_{n} + B\). Work out the product first, then add \(B\). Add matching entries, so each row gains its own entry of \(B\).
final.remember: Each state matrix comes from the one just before it: multiply by \(T\), then add any column.

a.q: A recurrence relation is \(S_{n+1} = TS_{n}\). Which calculation gives \(S_{2}\)?
a.why: Each state matrix comes from the one before it, so \(S_{2}\) comes from \(S_{1}\), with \(T\) written first. \(TS_{0}\) would give \(S_{1}\) instead.
a.clue: \(S_{2}\) is built from the state matrix just before it.

b.q: A fish pond has \(S_{n+1} = TS_{n} + B\), with \(T = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 & 0.3 \\ 0.2 & 0.7 \end{bmatrix}\), \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\) and \(S_{0} = \begin{bmatrix} 200 \\ 100 \end{bmatrix}\). What is \(S_{1}\)?
b.why: \(TS_{0} = \begin{bmatrix} 0.8 \times 200 + 0.3 \times 100 \\ 0.2 \times 200 + 0.7 \times 100 \end{bmatrix}\), which is \(\begin{bmatrix} 190 \\ 110 \end{bmatrix}\). Adding \(B = \begin{bmatrix} 10 \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\) entry by entry gives \(\begin{bmatrix} 200 \\ 110 \end{bmatrix}\). The option \(\begin{bmatrix} 190 \\ 110 \end{bmatrix}\) leaves out \(B\), \(\begin{bmatrix} 198 \\ 112 \end{bmatrix}\) adds \(B\) before multiplying, and \(\begin{bmatrix} 200 \\ 120 \end{bmatrix}\) adds 10 to both rows instead of 10 and 0.
b.clue: Multiply by \(T\) first, then add each entry of \(B\) to its matching row.
